Of the thirty-six thousand acres of Lake Tai, the moon speaks from the heart of the waves—to whom?
Ascending the hall, he said: "The river moon shines, the pine wind blows; throughout the eternal night and clear sky, what is there to do?

Master Yongjia had not a single tile to cover his head above, nor a spot of ground to stick a锥 (chui-needle) into below. Yet, at the crossroads of the street, he raised his voice and cried out aloud."
The land is vast and the people are sparse; those encountered are few. The mountain monk says to him: "Proceed slowly.
Even refined gold that has been smelted a hundred times must enter the red furnace once more."
Xie Liangban ascends the hall. With his whisk, he strikes once on the left and says, "The east is thus.
He strikes once on the right with the whisk and says, "The west is thus. Holding up a broken-legged cauldron, he says, "Everyone, let us support it together!
Raising it and then setting it down, he holds the whisk upright and says, "It is all not apart from this. A-ha-ha!
"The radishes of Zhenzhou have always been large.

[The Master] thanked the Head Seat for holding the whisk, then ascended the hall and said: "He shakes the Dharma thunder and beats the Dharma drum; jade-horned and golden-scaled, they raise clouds and spit mist.
Before the pivot of the mechanism, he topples Mount Lingxiao; grasping the entire earth, there is not an inch of soil left. Killing and giving life are fully wielded; all is leveled."
"You deceive the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Although this is so, tell me: what is the eye and mind of humans and devas? After a long silence, he said:
Returning from his journey of transformation, he ascended the hall. The scorching sun was at its peak as fiery clouds drifted by; then a heavy rain poured down, penetrating the four quarters.
The ripening grain wafts its fragrance and the people rejoice; even the mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees shine with brilliance. This is still merely for your enjoyment.
The samādhi of manifest activity. Now tell me: as for the matters within the gate of building and transforming, how is it? It was said: "This is a dragon;
he simply does not believe. Indeed, he has snatched the embroidered banner back home.
Ascending the hall to mark the conclusion of the retreat: The vast iron net opens wide on every side; through hundreds of cities, how many times have you gone and returned?
Who understands this bond formed over two thousand years? Once again, with three coins, you purchase a straw sandal.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "If no one speaks of the Buddha-dharma, though one possesses wisdom, one cannot realize it.
Fortunately, it is as level as a mirror; why then must it be bent like a fishing hook? Furthermore, the scriptures say: 'There is no dharma that can be spoken—this is called preaching the Dharma.
A crossbow capable of launching a thousand-jin bolt does not fire its trigger for a field mouse. Now, everyone, tell me: is there speaking, or is there no speaking? He struck his staff once.
He said, "It is not so, it is not so. He ascended the hall:
"The time is the ninth month of autumn; neither cold nor hot. The pebbles cry out to the autumn cicadas; the waning moon hangs from the thatched eaves."
Each person attains what is most appropriate; this is precisely the right moment. It is just as the Patriarch said: "Leaves fall and return to the root.
But when it comes to "having no mouth upon arrival," how is that? Kāśyapa’s face was yellowed; Bodhidharma’s teeth were missing.
Ascending the hall: Three times a day, nine times a day; one only knows the heat departs and the cold arrives, yet fails to realize that one has grown tottering and decrepit.
Take a step back to sever all subtle traces: after the hundred flowers have bloomed to their end, the yellow chrysanthemum remains at the eastern fence. Return to the hall for tea.
On the anniversary of Master Wude’s passing, he held up the incense and said: "Recalling those years long ago when I mistakenly sought him out, he exhausted his bitter and treacherous heart upon me.
Led astray again and again until I reached the summit of Lingxiao, the fire grew cold and the clouds grew chill, and my resentment deepened all the more.
An old grudge may be resolved but never should it be bound; yet what season is this now? How does striking a fist compare to the moment one receives a blow? This principle is clear."
To whom does he speak? He draws water from the ten-thousand-fathom depths of the dragon spring; he boils spring tea until it overflows like falling snow.
On the occasion of the Lantern Festival, he ascends the hall: "A single bowl at Mount Jing is the lantern of the Upper Yuan; it is not fashioned by gathering flowers or cutting patterns.
Casually picked up and hung out before the assembly, it pierces through the ghostly eyes of all quarters."
When the Venerable Zang-sou entered the Patriarchs’ Hall, he stepped across the Luoyang Bridge and ascended directly to the summit of the Wondrous Peak.
Grasping the black bamboo staff passed down from his ancestors, he stirred the thousand-fathom well of the Dragon Abyss. In four or five places thunder rolled and wind blew;

in eight, nine, or ten instances, there were the reflections of flowers and the moon in the water. To save others, he was truly dispassionate; who can lead him as he stands alone, liberated and holding up the staff? Though the bamboo staff—
The ancient statutes have been broken, yet what was heard and seen can still provoke deep reflection. Tell me, is Master Zang-sou alive or dead?
Under the cold light of the blue lamp at night, the incense smoke curls long through the day.
The Dragon King returns to his palace to offer incense. His vows are vast and profound; his majestic spirit is extraordinary. After six hundred years, the Buddhist monastery is restored;
throughout the thousand great worlds, its radiance illuminates the age. Acting as dews and rains, he nourishes the parched earth;

appearing as auspicious omens and blessings, he bestows fortune upon all beings near and far. His hidden merits are magnificent and secret; the Sage’s grace is beyond measure. With this new precious hall...

Returning to the capital, he received the imperial mandate to ascend the throne. With wisdom and integrity, he brooked no private interest. It was only because he had mistakenly received a prediction from Mount Ling that he now delivers this small sermon.
Compiled by the disciples Xingyou, Dezhen, Qionglin, and others during the summer retreat:
A phrase prior to sound, a single pivot beyond the extraordinary—neither falling into past or present, nor allowing for ordinary or sage.

Upon the peak of Mount Sumeru, within the radiance of the jade mirror, one dwells in *an-ga* (summer retreat) day after day, observing the *jin-zu* (foot-binding) precept at all times. The wind is calm and the waves are still; the ocean is tranquil.
The river is clear. Long-term and short-term; they are enjoyed equally. Do you all understand?
Leaning together on the same railing, yet leaning differently—how much wind from the Dragon King can such a person withstand?
Entering the Summer Retreat (*Varṣā*). To study the Way, one must first possess the cause for awakening. A thief has no fixed form;

he is bold and impulsive, yet like one who once raced a swift dragon boat. The blue-eyed barbarian monk laughs without ceasing. Although it is the idle ground of the old pavilion, when things meet their master, the eye stands upright.
Once you have come to exhaustion, only then will you rest. Within the shadows of the green willows are the oxen of Dai Song. Thus is the summer retreat.

Thus, observing the *jinzu* (the practice of standing on one foot), it is like casting oneself into fire; everything becomes fire. It is like melting an image to make gold—there is nothing that does not [transform].
If you allow branches to sprout from outside the joints, you will gaze toward Penglai with bated breath, for its Weak Waters lie thirty thousand *li* away.
If this is not yet the case, then seize the six giant turtles as they pass by your hand; do not let them go empty-handed to the Sea Mountains.
Entering the summer retreat, the wheel of the Dharma turns in an instant, and the eye of wisdom opens wide. Exercising unimpeded supernormal powers, one reveals inexhaustible wondrous functions;

completely transcending the jade mirror, one walks alone upon Mount Sumeru. There is no principle that is not extended, and every word is fully expressed. Since awakening occurs wherever one is, liberation must likewise occur wherever one is.
With the patched robe as one’s companion through the misty waters of a hundred cities, one wanders at ease, finding joy in one's practice and establishing a home.

It does not involve merit or achievement; it fully manifests one’s spirit and resolve. Even if one were to judge this from the standpoint of the Zen monk’s school, there would still be a gap of ninety days remaining.
But tell me, what excellence do these monks possess? After a long silence, he said: "If you do not sleep on the same bed, how can you know that there is a hole in the lining of the quilt?"
The retreat begins. The Great Way is beyond words; to speak of it is to commit slander. The picking up of the flower and the smile were but dragging through water and mud.

Facing the wall to settle the mind was merely following a mold and copying a pattern. Where ordinary and sage paths are severed, the body is encountered as entirely true. Vast and silent for ten thousand ages, there is nothing on which to rely.
In profound stillness, the divine light is never obscured. Along the road to Central India, thorns reach the heavens; amidst the moonlight upon the water, wind and clouds take on a strange aspect.
Can you yet believe this? Firmly securing the great barrier, there is nothing at all; with one long啸 (shout of laughter), the mist and fog deepen.
The retreat is concluded; the mouth of the cloth bag is opened. Heaven and earth are vast and open, cutting off the ten directions at once;
the six realms are clear as a breeze. Solitary and towering, not a blade of grass grows; steep and majestic, not a speck of dust remains. East, west, south, and north—no trace is left.
Transcending antiquity and surpassing the present, it stands vividly alive. Let De Shan and Linji peer as they may, there is no door for them to enter. What need is there to speak of long-term vows?
A short-term matter: strike it out with a single stroke. Why? Because the Buddha’s hand cannot block it; the human mind is as if indifferent. Regarding the formal retreat (*kaji*):
within the gate of the Patriarchs, the Way is cut off and men are sparse. At the edge of a ten-thousand-fathom cliff, those who meet [the truth] are few.
Magnificent and unimpeded, vast, penetrating, and harmoniously fused—if you attempt to deliberate upon this as "Buddha-dharma," you will inevitably fall into pits and ravines. Protecting life...
The summer retreat (*varṣā*). A sweatshirt that clings to the skin: easy to put on, difficult to take off. Carefully guarding the wax figure: it sticks to the teeth and gums;
easy to swallow, difficult to spit out. To contemplate and thereby know, to reflect and thereby understand—how much more refreshing than merely looking at plum blossoms to quench one's thirst!
As it is said: "Having felled the old pine tree before the gate, I have spent three or five years burning it."
The myriad affairs of state have come to rest; the thousand eyes open at once. Pressing straight ahead and lifting from the side, every shot hits the mark.
Floating and drifting, it falls into the empty courtyard; clearly and distinctly, cold springs pour forth in pure green. No merit is established; all saintly understandings are suddenly forgotten.

Unfurling and rolling up with ease, moving forward and backward with wondrous mastery. From this moment on, there is no returning; once you have returned, you shall find it. Who can vie for the misty scenery of the Five Lakes?
On the Winter Solstice, as the movements of the sun’s shadow shift and the days grow longer, the towering Feilai Peak remains exactly as it has been through kalpas.
Immovable and not shifting; unchanging and without difference. Against the rocky crags, dark shoots emerge from the earth; beyond the clouds, a thousand peaks lock in their cold greenery.
The Way of the noble person and the Way of the petty person naturally wane and wax. Thus is the Zen of the Tathāgata and the Zen of the Patriarchs.
"There is not even enough space for the point of a锥 (chui) to stand. At night, the old Wang of East Village burns paper money; wild ghosts and idle spirits vie with one another in their pride.
If this were under the gate of a patch-robed monk, it would not take more than a single sneeze to ensure their souls flee and their hearts shatter.

But tell me, what excellence does the gate of a patch-robed monk possess? After a long silence, he said: "It is simply because of the error at Shaoshi that the fragrance has spread; five leaves from a single flower."
The fragrance strikes the nostrils.
On New Year’s Eve, on the level and real path, one knocks and rattles at the gate and courtyard. Vertically and horizontally encompassing all, responding universally to the high and the low.
At the crown of the head, it stands upright; beneath the heels, not a single thread is revealed. Meeting a Buddha, he covers his face; hearing the Dharma, he rinses his mouth.

When all traces of the sage are exhausted and removed, the wind blows and the grass bows. Only at the depth of night does one see the person holding the needle; leaning against the railing, one quietly gazes upon the snow on a thousand mountains.
Let spring return as it will, let the year end as it may; let the old be replaced by the new.
The three hundred and sixty days of last year were just so; the three hundred and ninety days of this year are just so. Whether more or less, there is no surplus, nor is there any lack.
Nothing lacking. Look; pressed on until reaching the point of convergence, one realizes it is already the thirtieth day of the twelfth month.
Ahead, there is no village to reach; behind, there is no inn to catch. Such is the traveler on the road—how can they ever arrive home?

Therefore, the ancients said: "When the Way is without mind, it accords with man; when man is without mind, he accords with the Way. If you understand this inner meaning, one grows old and yet does not age.
Old Age. Do you all wish to see that which does not grow old? It is precisely because it is so utterly clear that what is attained is delayed.
At the winter solstice, before a single stroke had yet taken form, there was a vast, undifferentiated expanse. Once names and forms began to manifest, the black bean sprouted its seed.
Days grew short and nights long; cold came and heat passed away. From the very beginning, whether Buddhas or Patriarchs, they have all proclaimed this from within the void.
A branch sprouts from outside the joints. Plucking a flower, crossing on a single reed; windless waves arise, tossing the four oceans.

All people throughout the world have no place to set foot. Tonight at Lingyin, I wish to reveal a message to you all at the moment when the yin is about to dissolve yet has not fully dissolved, and the yang is about to grow yet has not yet grown.
(He strikes the meditation staff once. "A thousand peaks are locked."
A cold hue; from a single tree, dark fragrance drifts.
The retreat is concluded. The mouth of the hemp sack is opened; the ten directions are unobstructed. Speaking a single phrase offhand, it blocks the throat of the Old Barbarian.
Taking a single step with one’s feet, it tramples through the backbone of Gautama. For all people throughout the great earth, there is no place to stand or act.

The four noble ones and the six classes of ordinary beings are all tongue-tied and have their allotted shares. Thus it is said: "For ninety days, the feet are restrained; one draws lines on the ground to make a prison.

For three months, one dwells in retreat; one strikes at emptiness to produce sound. If one is a heroic superior person whose spirit and bearing startle the multitude—like a golden-scaled fish leaping through the net, swimming amidst the waves;
like a fine hawk escaping its cage, soaring through the clouds and mists—this is indeed so. Yet, as for this very point:
Where there is not a single blade of grass for ten thousand miles, as soon as one steps out the door, it is all grass. Furthermore, what kind of person can walk such a path?
Ask Old Wang, north of the river and south of the river; one doubt leads to another doubt.
Winter Solstice: Seizing it as it comes, one employs it immediately. Casting forth the night-bright pearl in the open light, the Great Gate of Bestowal stands wide open.

Who, directly beneath it, can offer a matching price? Whether in the rhythmic exchange of the gate and courtyard or wherever one touches, all is true. Directly confronting the critical moment, it universally responds to all levels, high and low.
Cold and icy; the entire body is free of reliance. Steep and towering; not even a speck of dust can stand. When exhausted, there is change; with change, there is penetration.
Once the single stroke has taken form, the thunder beneath the earth has already roared. Yin wanes and Yang grows; flowers bloom upon the iron tree. Fragrant winds blow in all directions.
Heaven and earth are vast and empty; for one who has realized their true nature, how should they act? The frosty sky, the moon has set, and night is half spent.
Who shares this cold reflection in the clear pool?

At the arrival of the seasonal solstice, five peaks stand steeply aloft and ten thousand ravines are chilled by clouds. The manifestation of reality is fully realized; face and features are entirely revealed.
Having trodden this ground, let the yin reach its extreme and yang arise; let shards and rubble gleam with brilliance, while the myriad phenomena lose their luster.
Be they stones large or small, bamboo straight or crooked, the sky is high with clouds and the water appears because of the moon. It is the numinous clarity.
Vastly transparent, ancient and modern are merged as one. To simply proceed in this manner and sit waiting for the cold ashes to subside is ultimately not the superior strategy.
If you are a man of heroic spirit, a great practitioner who has committed the five heinous acts, you must overturn the traditional gateways of the patriarchs and establish your own living livelihood.
Before the winter solstice, the plum blossoms are sparse; wait further for the spring breeze to grace the old branches. Regarding this:
the single path leading upward is directly manifest before one. Its functioning never halts; it dwells in the markless.

Heaven and earth are themselves heaven and earth; sun and moon are themselves sun and moon. In their encompassing, supporting, darkening, and brightening, not even a hair’s breadth can be altered. They embrace and harmonize all existence.
Beyond the phenomenal world, all things shine in equal clarity. Following the teaching that when Yin reaches its extreme, Yang is born, let one simply allow the cold to come and the heat to go.
Thus, for twenty-one days, the Elder Gautama contemplated such matters, searching for a way to open his mouth;

yet, alas, he could find none. Principle can subdue even a leopard. [The Master] strikes the staff once and says: "At this point, if you can turn your body around and bring forth [your realization]..."

The vital energy is awakened; the eyes are opened; one has reached the destination. Three thousand cranes from Liaodong and nine ten-thousand-mile journeys of the Peng bird—all the world gathered together is but the size of a grain of millet.
Is this not a life lived with full vigor, the accomplishment of the great man’s enterprise? If it is not yet so, then heed this.
Once the plum blossoms have departed, there is no news of them;
only the spring breeze can call them back. The Year’s End: This year ends this very night; next year arrives tomorrow. Cold departs with one night gone; spring follows as the fifth watch returns.
But suppose the spring does not return and the cold does not depart—how would you all deal with that? Beneath Mount Lingxiao.
Zhuo struck his staff once and said: "This entire field of land does not belong to yin or yang; how could it be constrained by the workings of creation?
The sun and moon cannot illuminate it; cold and heat cannot invade it. It is without change or transition; it neither comes nor goes.

Reaching upward to the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception and extending downward to the limits of the empty wheel and the waters' edge, it is utterly boundless and without limit, not separated by even a hair’s breadth. Throughout the three periods of time..."
The Buddha’s traces of activity have ceased; north, south, east, and west are all as they were before. There is no ox from Beichan to be cooked, nor wine from Qingyuan to be poured.
Before and behind the mountain, the wild foxes sing the village field music with every cry.
Joyful indeed it is, yet who knows that on this eve of the year’s end, there remains one who has not yet returned?
A Verse Lament for the Late Master Huìyán, the Celestial Youth:
Enmity and favor, layer upon layer, divided yet undivided; Returning once more, the man of old is no longer seen. Before the pavilion, the herons rest in elegant stillness.
The moon shines on; the west wind blows across the white water lilies.
I bid farewell to Master Wen as he travels to Tai and Tang.

The full brilliance of his literary talent is manifest upon the tip of his staff. Mounts Wu and Waters of Chu—his inspiration flows boundlessly. The sound of the river has all night hastened his departure.
Form. Only when the stone bridge is trampled and severed does one finally rest.

When Guest Manager Sen was sent to pitch camp by the banks of the Qingyuan Creek, the spring breeze gathered thickly, revealing the banners and spears. Who would have known that he was calling the guests for tea?
Though ten thousand distinctions and a thousand differences exist, they all return to the One Way.
As the monk You of Gaoyou departs for his Great Journey through life and death, he is utterly destitute yet has not yet reached home; he turns his head toward the hundred and ten cities.
In the region to the south of Great Huainan there are high sands.

As the monk Yunshang departs, a sun and moon hang from the tip of his *zhizhang* staff; the mountains and rivers are carried upon the heels of his straw sandals. When anyone asks him about my house, [he points to these].
The matter: Before Vulture Peak lies Cold Spring.
Sending off Master Jian—Jian was already late by a hair’s breadth; even lightning and sparks are difficult to pursue. A single touch at Vulture Peak and he turns back.
Go! Never again will you place [the brush] upon your eyebrows over your eyes.
Deliver this to Master Xian of the State;
my Way has from the beginning been free of right and wrong. Among those who have attained it, Xian is foremost. A single smile before the flowers, and he immediately returns.
First: This journey to West River is eight thousand *li*.
Entrust the Dharma robe to the attendant Qionglin;
the burden of Yangqi is neither light nor heavy. Once it has been taken upon the shoulder, proceed at once. Clench your teeth and maintain the correct focus.
The command: To roll up or unroll, to kill or give life, acting with total freedom and mastery.

Having shown the three white foods, he has completely cast away the extraordinary flavors upon the tip of the hermit’s tongue; pines, bamboos, mist, and clouds become his simple companions. Though he possesses a mouth, he does not swallow the three periods of time.
Buddha. A single day of wind, moon, and dew is desolate and wild.
Sending off a monk, he sits gaunt; his pure conduct is fitting for the mountain stream. His patched robe is crisp and clean, damp with the blue mist. The spring light has entirely followed his staff.
Depart! You leave behind the evening mountains where the cries of monkeys cease.
Sending the junior disciple Chunchi away to travel and study Chan is no small matter;
his resolve must be as firm as iron and stone. He shall rely upon a hundred cities until he is left without support.
Leaning back, he turns his head and returns; a painful punch awaits upon his arrival.
To Layman Ni:
Amidst all dust and phenomena lies the firm and dense body; in every particle of dust, the person of original nature suddenly appears. Know that beyond this, there is nothing else.
The Buddha. Wild birds and mountain flowers are uniquely springtime.
Showing the horse’s road-bell:
practicing Zen is the business of a man of honor. A fine steed has never required a whip. All six windows are open; heaven and earth are revealed.
Vast! Ten thousand *li* of cloudless, single-piece sky.
Sending off a monk returning to Tiantai:
leaping from within the waves of Longmen, A chilling wind arises and the spirit of his domain is clear. Returning to Shiqiao, you shall see for yourself.
Look! At the tip of the staff, the sound of surging waves still lingers.
As I see off K'ai, the *vīnā* master:
rolling along the bottom, the angry waves are a thousand fathoms of snow; turning through the void, the bright moon is an autumn sky. In parting, do not speak of [the empty]— [The text ends here.]
The crypt. Clearly visible upon the staff of your house.
Sent by the attendant who gathers refuse, it was picked up from a heap of sweepings. Before the flowers, one cannot help but see a smile bloom. At Vulture Peak, this was written as a parting gift.
These words remain as a source of calamity for the monastic community.
I send my junior disciple Chunzhen to visit Xuedou’s Qianzhangyan, where ten thousand layers of hanging clouds gather;
there the old dragon lies high and still, rarely seen even by those who seek him. You, my son, now resolve to scale his scales.
Horn. Do not look back as the snow-waves fly before the crags.
I send this to Layman Zhou Yizhai, while briefly addressing Tang Dongjian:
"I envy Yizhai for going and yet returning; by the stream, not a speck of dust remains. His lofty wind is chillingly bright, illuminating the present."
In ancient times, there was one whose mouth spoke not, yet his voice resembled thunder.
Upon seeing the Honored One returning to Jianzhou, his vision was clear and his realization intimate;
he turned his body directly upon the edge of a sword and returned again to the cloud-connected mountain passes and galleries.
"Head! You have already become a person of the past, no longer the person you once were.
The monk has long since been sent to Xuefeng;
he died on South Mountain at Bianbi long ago. Why do you toil through such rugged terrain to seek him out? Gather him up in a bottomless basket!"
It is obtained; there is no harm in taking the staff-head back home.
I often recall the Scholar of the West Lake’s house with its ink-plum blossoms; their sparse branches and cold buds lean and slant of their own accord. That single piece of brilliance from that time—
The matter is simply that there is a lack of pure fragrance, not a lack of flowers.
If you harbor great doubt and this mind remains undecided, you must resolve it. Once resolved, whom would you ask now? In daily life, one stands forthright and majestic, without direction.
Turning one's back, let the partridges cry at will among the spring mountains.
At Mount Jin, bricks are repaired on the shore;
ten thousand li of the Long River surge with golden turtles. Standing firm in the midstream, its majestic momentum is bold. Let it be released directly so that the foundation is secured.
Stable. Let the winds and waves rise from all eight directions;

the Tripitaka seals are clearly revealed when the printing blocks are cast forth. It is only because the eyes of those weary in life have not yet opened. One must shatter a single mote of dust to turn it over.
It emerges. From the sands of the great trichiliocosm, clouds and thunder arise.
The descendants of the sutra-burner have, for a generation, deliberated in error. Shake loose the rotten entrails of Gautama; the fire of samādhi smokes out the three poisons.
Fire! How could such private household matters be broadcast to outsiders?

With clear coin for hospitality, a short staff and a light satchel, one expresses the sentiment of a recluse. Why do you pass through Qianqing with such bustling purpose? Enter the gate to eat a meal, then depart.
Go! Do not say that the mountains and waters of Wozhou are green.

I present this to the Master, the Daoist Physician of Teeth, who has attained the Way; he can heal toothaches so they no longer ache with a mere snap of the fingers. Now that I am eighty years old, I eat my fill.
Throughout his years, he never once bit into a single grain of rice.
The calligrapher’s strokes, horizontal and vertical, were all freshly cast. The "zhi-hu-ye-zhe" turned into pure spirit; it was simply a matter of distinguishing black from white.
In this state, examine those who exhaustively seek out characters and count ink-streaks;

when the labor of shaving the head reaches its true application, there is no more stumbling or hesitation. When mind and hand correspond, one knows it for oneself; when even a hair’s breadth is exhausted, the news arrives.
Exhausted! It does not hinder the eyes; yet eyebrows are placed upon them once more.
This is the true eulogy of the image of him emerging from the mountains.
He cast aside the honor and glory of ten thousand chariots; for six years on the Snowy Peaks, he endured hunger and cold. Upon seeing the morning star, he turned his head back;
yet in the end, as before, he was deceived by his own eyes.
Avalokiteśvara casts his body across the sea of suffering, light as a single leaf. Though black winds blow him down, he moves freely in all directions.
To cause those in perilous places to turn their heads back, the moon rises over Potalaka at the edge of the heavens.

The Spirit of the Horse-Dealer’s Daughter possesses a pure and lofty air; her hair is like green clouds in a small bun. She has deceived every fine young man until they have recited the entire Lotus Sūtra.
In the end, no marriage was joined; the moonlight on the golden sand shines in vain.
Bodhidharma (2):
In the land of Chu, during the Taiping era, he contemplated crossing the sea; when calamity arose in China, he came toward the East.
Had he not encountered the Son of Heaven of Liang at that time, he would have been nothing more than one buried deep in the earth.
How could the Imperial Edict of Emperor Liang have been in vain? When private trade in stagnant goods flourishes, prices only rise higher.
Amidst the whistling reeds under the moon of Mount Xiong’er, even today the great earth remains a surging tide.

Master Bao’s scissors, whisk, and ruler hang high; his golden staff is suspended. Selling dogs while hanging up sheep—much empty talk and little substance. He caused Emperor Wu to chase Bodhidharma across the river;
from this point on, the "five petals and one flower" became a chaotic mess. I bow my head to the Twelve-Faced Avalokiteśvara.
Who among those facing forward can recognize it? [口@力]. The Baguī (Sack) refuses to dwell in the Tuṣita Inner Palace;
with staff over shoulder, he carries the sack into the dust of the mundane world. One knows not why he opens his mouth to laugh.
People will laugh at you when you are born into the human realm. Aha-ha! Keep your belly wide open and wait for them.
No one recognizes this Pig-Headed Monk, the Holy One of Jinhua; when they meet him, they simply ask for his head to eat. Turning back, he returns by the old path.
Returning home, a spring breeze scatters the fragrance in disarray.
The oyster-fisher does not seek whales or turtles; he gathers only oysters. Having tasted their flavor, his joy is all the greater. He picks them up and stuffs them into his mother-born mouth.
Mouth. A segment of scenery belongs to the master of the house.
Hanshan has no skill; he loves to compose poems. One phrase—few people know it. Listen silently and serenely as the pine wind blows.
Shide picked up a broom for sweeping; its use was intimate. Cease pointing and explaining—it is all in vain toil. The original ground is utterly free of even a speck of dust.
—Yaoshan.
Water in a jar. A sutra beneath a pine tree. When someone comes to ask, present it face-to-face. White clouds have dispersed;
the autumn sky is blue. — Lánzàn.
The mountains are deep and secluded; the path is like a sheep’s gut. Imperial edicts descend upon purple clay; the imperial ink is still fragrant. It is reported that we folk are busy roasting taro.
Deshan.
Carrying my commentaries and sub-commentaries on my travels, I bore a great burden of indignation. When I stumbled upon Longtan, my lifelong aspirations were not yet satisfied.
At the moment the paper lamp was blown out, I struck the very nose of my mother’s birth. Thereupon, I took a torch and burned away those idle, old papers.
From this point on, he was filled with indignation as he sought his enemy; a single white staff shook heaven and earth.
Sitting upright atop the peaks of Linji and Huangbo, he opened his mouth only to bite into raw iron; turning over at Gaoyuan Ford, he was just like—
Brandishing the staff to strike at the moon—since then, he has understood. With empty hands and bare fists, he uses one wedge to drive out another. Distinctly so!
The "Unranked True Person" is a dry dung-pestle.

Master Fuguang’s vast and majestic breeze of compassion pervades the universe; his flowing eloquence pours forth like the four rivers’ clarity. He wears the entire body of Vairocana’s ocean-seal upon him;
fragrant clouds of *udumbara* flowers fill the imperial capital.
Master Xutang was like a playful sea monster or a fierce tiger emerging from the mountains; his eyes overspread heaven and earth, and his spirit swallowed the Buddhas and patriarchs.

When he established strict rules and regulations, even a drop of water turned to ice; when he raised the supreme teaching, he transcended both past and present. He presided over nine famous monasteries and three times received imperial edicts.
I have no shame before the man who faced the wall in his youth; he simply had one more tooth in his mouth.
Great Master Xuecheng and Master Yinfeng both had younger sisters; I too have a younger sister. Although we each traveled our own paths, in the end, we arrived at the same time.
Flowers bloom and fall by the eastern city wall; sons and grandsons succeed one another through the generations.
I praise myself for having painted this with full measure, yet let us believe only half of it. From tail to head, there is no shore at all—just a single point of the "ghost-eye."
The eyes: black beans can never truly replace them. Walking slowly and with measured steps atop the Five Peaks, a single bright moon soars through the Milky Way.
Elder Qionglong Sen invited him to show his true face;
yet it cannot be captured in a painting, for he possesses no artifice at all. He has taken up the heavy burden of Yangqi.
Before the staff and the shout, who dares to conceive? Thrown crosswise and cast upward, the sand-pot is shattered. At the summit of Tongxuan Peak, a pure breeze arises.
At the request of the attendant Qionglin of Japan.
A hundred uglinesses, a thousand clumsinesses—there is no dharma that can be spoken. A single fist is as hard as raw iron; when opened, it illuminates the rising sun;
when clenched, heaven and earth turn pitch black. You enemies, do not give rise to evil associations!
The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye has been extinguished by the blind donkey.
The junior master Chunzhen requested that his efforts be meticulous and thorough;
even brush and ink could not reach it. When the true command is fully raised, even a Buddha does not recognize it. It is utterly poisonous and loathsome to others;
it is entrusted to those who destroy their families and commit the five heinous crimes.
The junior disciple Chunyuan requested to take his seat upon the folding chair. Wind arose through the ten thousand ravines; he spoke without speaking and acted without acting.
Before the sound, there was a clear source, yet ultimately not even a trace of the character "Yuan" remained.
The junior disciple Chunmi requests:
His head is white and his eyebrows and beard are white; there is not a speck of ink in his breast. He speaks of Chan without conforming to the times, doing nothing but pointing to his chest and ribs.
This profound meaning is clearly manifest right here before you; why wait for the future to ask Maitreya?
Yunwei invited this man of cruel poison;
originally faceless, difficult to portray. A single stroke of the brush offends, blinding the true eye of the monk and exterminating the lineage of the Old Barbarian.
The calamities plaguing the monastic groves have not yet ceased; all at once, they are entrusted to Yunwei of Qingjiang.

The attendant Yì requested: "His countenance is truly loathsome. His mind is as straight as a ruler; he makes no distinction between this and that. What loss or gain could there be? He does not treat the Buddha-dharma as mere worldly sentiment.
Let him do as he pleases, even if his broken sand-pot lies in utter disorder."

The old attendant before the quarters requests that your mind be as straight as a bowstring and your nature as swift as an arrow. Turning the hand over and turning it back; the face of the sun and the face of the moon. Striking it out bit by bit and piece by piece until the sand pot is broken.
The view of self, the view of others, the view of sentient beings, and the view of a life-span.
For this minor Buddhist service, the attendant Zhao holds the torch;
with ten strikes of the mallet, all myriad functions cease. Silent illumination shines forth, and everything is suddenly cast down—purely naked and bare.
Brilliant! In the end, one seeks the traces of birth and death in vain. Before every door stands a torch. Master Tandan holds the torch;
when the myriad shadows are stripped away, the first Yang arrives. To emerge from death and enter life is like a game. Master Tandan, cease!
Deliberation: Let the dilapidated hut be consumed by wild fires. A single *tánhuā* (dharma-flower) wafts its fragrance to the nose.
Chén Xīnjiè held the torch;
having become a monk in his youth, he passed away in his youth. The *tánhuā* has borne fruit before ever seeing the frost. It is not the autumn wind that hastens them.
Urgent! The mouth of the sack opens; with staff in hand, one is busy. Where there is a Buddha, do not dwell; where there is no Buddha, pass by swiftly.
The iron gates of birth and death are all crushed through. But tell me, after they are crushed through, what is it like?
I call it fire; you must not call it fire.
The Venerable Xiu held the torch, defying the snow and withstanding the frost;
the pines and cypresses stand alone in their excellence. Leaves fall and return to the root; when he came, he had no mouth.

When the ancient masters speak thus, where has there ever been birth and death? They burn it all away until nothing remains but a single heap of ash—behold the divine light piercing the Ox and Dipper constellations.
The first treasury keeper (a native of Fuzhou; the third-generation descendant of Mian) held up a torch and drew a circle, saying:
"Just this very thing emerged from the broken sand-pot, manifest and true. For eighty-one years, its utility has been inexhaustible;
the entire Great Canon of Teachings cannot fully describe it. Casting down his mountain-ax, he laughed and roamed in the purity [of the mountains].
The spring is white and pure; sharp shackles and famous tethers cannot restrain it. Its nostrils reach the vast heavens, unrecognized by men.
It comes without trace and goes without mark. Within the flash of a stone struck by lightning, the years and months are long. Even were it an iron snake, it could not pierce through.

Standing upright as the Elder, entering the stupa, not a single speck of dust can be established. A silver mountain and an iron wall; the adamantine barrier of birth and death. Even a Buddha does not recognize it—this is for those of unyielding bone.
Enter here. Master Gong entered the stupa to pass into parinirvāṇa.
Now, Liu Tiemo—this very man of iron bones—disdains the Buddha and refuses to act as one.
Once gone, he returns; in the end, there are never two. Having turned over within the furnace, he was again pressed down before the Many-Buddhas Stupa.
The attendant held the torch.

Wealth and honor do not envy the Three Terraces; in studying the Way, one must equal the Elder Lu. Having trampled through the sturdy gates of birth and death, what need is there to speak of Danxia raking the weeds?
It is well thus; it is well not thus. In the twelfth month, fire burns the mountains;
snow embraces a thousand peaks at dawn.
The Old Official of Ten Karmas holds the torch;

coming and going in dreams, he does not remember autumn. He knows only that his youthful head has turned white. Hearing the sutras, listening to the Dharma, and dwelling in reliance upon the Sangha, he is unrestrained by birth and death and has attained freedom.
His straw sandals are tightly fastened; his entire being is elegant and refined. There is no need to poke at the fire.
Seeking a floating bubble.
An attendant holding a torch stood at my left;
another attendant stood at my right. With palms joined, he stepped forward; with hands crossed, he withdrew behind. At the mortar-house, the rice was white as he turned over his body.
Not falling into the trap of Huangmei; not writing a verse; not transmitting the robe. Holding up a torch: behold a flake of snow fly upon the red furnace.
A Verse on Parting from the World.
The eighty-second year. Boarding a bottomless boat, he returns, overturning it; the bright moon fills the sky.

*Biography*.
The Master’s name was Pudu; he was a native of Jiangdu in Wuyang. His style was Xuzhou, and his surname was Shi.
Initially, in Danyang, there was a Rhetuo from Min who had white hair and a dark face; over eighty years of age, he sat motionless morning and evening like a withered stump.
He struck the *qing* gong to perform rites before the image of Potalaka. He constantly recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in silence.

He had previously been acquainted with his grandfather while traveling between the regions of Jing and Wu; whenever he carried his almsbowl across the Huai River, he would invariably go to his grandfather’s home to stay overnight. His grandfather treated him with exceptional kindness.
One morning, after the early cooking was finished, the grandmother sat in the main hall. The dhūta came from outside and went straight toward the delivery room.
The grandmother, wondering at his reason for doing so, followed his tracks to the place of birth, but he was nowhere to be found. She then sent a household servant to the man’s residence to inquire;
the resident said, "At the third strike of the morning bell, the dhūta sat upon his square couch and departed. Afterward—

Upon his birth, a rare fragrance emanated from his chamber and permeated all the neighboring houses, resembling the scent of opening lotus buds. After some time, when he reached the age of one year, he saw the pagoda of Mount Jinshan across the river and was immediately able to join his palms in reverence.
Whenever a bhikṣu guest passed by his door, he would invariably reach out and grasp the hem of the monk’s robe.
He was filled with joy. As he grew slightly older, although he studied the classics of poetry and ritual as well as secular books, he lacked any intention to enter worldly life.
His mother, realizing that his long-held resolve could not be overturned, ordered him to leave the household life at Tianning Monastery in the prefecture; he was twelve years old at the time.

More than two years passed before he met General Bi again, who was providing a meal for the monastics at the monastery. Upon conversing with him, the General marveled greatly at him and said to his steward:
"This boy is short and sturdy, yet his voice resonates like a bell. In the future, he will be a formidable leader within the Dharma. He then took him back to the capital.
At that time, he longed for the tranquility of a forest hermitage; thus, he shaved his head daily and extensively gathered for both Chan meditation and doctrinal lectures.
The one of great virtue [Shou-nan] served as his witness; Jingci’s Shaolin Song performed the tonsure ceremony; Lingyin’s Tie-niu Yin conferred the robe upon him;
and Longxi Zuxin of Dongtang Monastery in his native district served as his preceptor for receiving the precepts. Having completed these rites, he entered the monastic order.
He returned to the Eastern Hall and served with diligent faith for five years.

One night, he suddenly stirred up his resolve and said to his colleagues, "I observe that since the time of Bodhidharma and Shen Guang, those who galloped like dragons and tigers, or soared like phoenixes and peng-birds, were all ordinary people of the mundane world."
"He has directly ascended to the ancestral seat. He was able to do this; am I then unable to do so? At dawn, he took up a straw rain-hat and hastened to Tien-niu Yin (Iron Ox Seal).

The Master [Tien-niu] encouraged his journey with a discourse on the Dharma. From there, he traveled extensively throughout the regions east and west of the Yangtze River and north and south of Lake Dongting.
At that time, Master Wude Tong was propagating the Way of Songyuan at Jianfu Temple in Fanyang.
Consequently, [Zhaozhou] resolved to seek instruction from him, fulfilling his original vow. Whether Tong moved to Foyan or Huazang, Zhaozhou always carried his bundle with him.
Once, while entering the room for private instruction, Tong asked, "Who is it that does not take companionship with the myriad dharmas? The Master replied, "Beneath the golden incense burner."
Tie Kunlun said, "I thought this short man had some merit; it turns out your understanding is such as this. The Master bowed deeply and said, "I thank the Abbot for his witness.
From then on, they were like a magnet and iron in their accord. Whether the Dharma duties were difficult or easy, he was tested through them all.
After several years, he took his leave of Tong and went to put what he had attained to the test in the world. He studied under Tiantong Huirong, Guang, and Daci.

Shi Yanlian and Huqiu Shishi Di perceived his extraordinary capacity at their first meeting, realizing he was beyond compare. Consequently, they retained him to oversee monastic affairs among the three masters.
At the beginning of the Chunyou era, Zhao Xin’an, the Governor of Jiankang, earnestly invited him to take charge of the world [as abbot] at Bānshān.
He then raised the incense [of the lineage], succeeding Wude at Jīnsān in Run, Lùyuàn in Tan, Shūsān in Fu, and Sū...
This was how he succeeded his master. Ascending through these successive stages, the Master resided at Jīnshān (Golden Mountain), while Chījue (Chizhu) resided at Yùshān (Jade Mountain).

There is a tradition that when he addressed the assembly amidst the snow one night, he uttered the verse: "The river wind stirs the jade whisk; the solitary peak is not white, yet its spirit turns ever more brilliant.
Chījue was greatly astonished and personally boarded a boat to visit him, saying, "I, an old man, shall yield three stations to you; your excellence is supreme."

His virtue was such that it caused people to revere him in this way. He subsequently retired from his duties and resided in the West Hall of Lingyin Monastery, where his reputation grew increasingly widespread.
During the Jingding era, the Grand Preceptor, Duke of Wei, Jia, reported the Master’s name to the Emperor.

Consequently, he was appointed to fill the vacant position at Zhong Tianzhu Monastery for six years. Later, when the retired monk Ning of Lingyin passed away, Duke Wei again petitioned on the Master’s behalf.
Jisuo presided over his temple for seven years; those who came to him gathered like rivers meeting and clouds piling up, and his dharma assembly was renowned as being exceptionally flourishing.
At one time, there was someone who, harboring private resentment, brought harm upon the high officials of the court; the Master immediately abandoned the position and departed without looking back.

In the *dingchou* year of the Zhizhi era (1297), he received an imperial decree to go to Mount Jing. Following the great conflagration that had swept the mountain clean, he exhausted his heart and strength to plan its restoration.
